title: Impact of the Wood‐Burning Justa Stove Intervention on Inflammation in a Stepped‐Wedge Randomised Trial in Rural Honduras
content:
Abstract

Cleaner cooking solutions have been promoted to reduce household air pollution (HAP), but it remains unclear whether these reductions improve health. To understand potential biological pathways, we examined how the Justa intervention—an engineered wood-burning cookstove that reduced HAP concentrations at or near health-relevant targets within our trial—affected markers of systemic injury and inflammation in rural Honduran women. We recruited 230 female cooks for a 3-year randomised stepped-wedge trial that included 6 repeated measures of exposure and health outcomes every ∼6 months. We measured 24-hr personal and kitchen concentrations of fine particulate matter and black carbon (BC) and estimated long-term average exposures. Inflammatory biomarkers (i.e., primary outcome: C-reactive protein (CRP); secondary outcomes: interleukins 1beta, 6, 8 [IL-1β, IL-8, and IL-6], and tumor necrosis factor-alpha [TNF-α]) were measured via dried blood spots. Linear mixed models were used in intent-to-treat (i.e., assigned stove use as the exposure-of-interest), “per-protocol” (i.e., self-reported stove use as the exposure-of-interest), and HAP exposure-response analyses. We did not observe associations between assigned use of the Justa intervention compared to traditional stove use and inflammatory marker levels (e.g., CRP (n = 1,103): −7.32%, 95% Confidence Interval: −18.54, 5.44; IL-8 (n = 1,224): 4.50%, 95% CI: −2.27, 11.74). Similar null results were observed in per-protocol analysis. In the exposure-response analyses, we observed that higher HAP exposures were associated with higher levels of IL-8, TNF-α, and IL-1β but not CRP and IL-6. Although assigned use of the intervention did not impact inflammation, we provide evidence of positive exposure-response associations for several secondary biomarkers.
